title: "Joint targets for β-lactam / β-lactamase inhibitor pairs"
description: "Why ceftazidime–avibactam-style combinations need simultaneous success rules — and why averaging two PTAs is not joint target attainment."

A β-lactam/β-lactamase inhibitor (BL/BLI) pair is not one drug with two names. One component usually provides antibacterial exposure; the other protects that exposure from enzymes. Adequacy is therefore often a **joint** event.

::: {.callout-note}
## Scope
Simulation logic for combination PK/PD. Example framing inspired by ceftazidime–avibactam-style problems; not product-specific clinical advice.
:::

## Two clocks, one decision

Suppose:

- Drug A (β-lactam) must satisfy a free-exposure target vs MIC,
- Drug B (inhibitor) must stay above a threshold that preserves A’s activity.

Patient-level success is:

\[
\mathbf{1}\{A \text{ succeeds}\} \land \mathbf{1}\{B \text{ succeeds}\}
\]

not the average of the two success indicators.

## Common modeling mistakes

1. **Collapse to one analyte** — simulating only the β-lactam because “that is the antibiotic.”
2. **Report mean(PTA_A, PTA_B)** as if it were joint attainment.
3. **Ignore correlation** — clearances of A and B may covary; independent draws can misstate joint tails.
4. **Borrow incompatible thresholds** — inhibitor targets from a different matrix, population, or regimen without labeling.

## A clean joint workflow

1. Simulate both concentration–time profiles in each virtual subject.
2. Apply component-specific free targets.
3. Mark joint success only when both pass.
4. Build PTA vs MIC (or vs scenario grid) from the joint indicator.
5. Optionally weight by MIC ecology → joint CFR.

This is the same philosophy used in provenance-aware CAZ-AVI style evidence-composite work: components stay separate until a joint rule is applied deliberately.

## Takeaway

For BL/BLI pairs, **protection failure is regimen failure** even when the β-lactam curve looks beautiful alone. Joint PTA is an intersection, not an average.
